title: How Occam's Razor Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain Occam's Razor, the philosophical heuristic that among competing explanations the simplest is usually preferred, and that it should not add entities without necessity. They cover its roots in Aristotle and Robert Grosseteste, the life of William of Ockham (Franciscan monk, excommunicated, sheltered by Emperor Louis IV in Munich), the medieval synthesis championed by Thomas Aquinas, and the Lorentz vs. Einstein relativity debate and positivism (Ernst Mach). They discuss how skeptics and creationists, atheists, and others misuse the razor to dismiss ideas, why simplicity is subjective and human-made, and examples like ghost photos, neural network decision trees, geocentrism vs. heliocentrism, and art. The episode opens with a tour announcement (Salt Lake City and Phoenix dates) and closes with listener mail from Claire Sutherland about North Korea's official condemnation of her Australian newspaper's Olympic medal tally graphic.

segments.title: Tour announcement and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh announces added 2018 tour dates in Salt Lake City (Grand Theater, October 23) and Phoenix (Van Buren, October 24), then the hosts riff on mustaches and rosemary.

segments.title: What Occam's Razor is
segments.summary: Introduction to Occam's Razor as a heuristic that the simplest explanation is usually best, with the Latin formulations: principle of plurality and principle of parsimony. They debate whether the two are different.

segments.title: William of Ockham's life and the church
segments.summary: Biography of William of Ockham, a Franciscan monk and rationalist in England (c. 1285 to 1349) who clashed with Pope John XXII, was excommunicated, and fled to Munich under Emperor Louis IV. The attribution of the razor's wording is questioned; John Duns Scotus and a 19th-century mathematician are mentioned.

segments.title: Aristotle, Grosseteste, and medieval synthesis
segments.summary: The idea traces to Aristotle and was expanded by Robert Grosseteste. The hosts contrast Ockham's rationalism with the medieval synthesis of Thomas Aquinas, in which all knowledge was thought to come from God.

segments.title: Empiricism and the Lorentz vs. Einstein debate
segments.summary: Discussion of empirical evidence. Lorentz explained relativity's effects with changes in the ether, while Einstein gave a simpler explanation without the ether, which won out. The hosts also cover positivism and Ernst Mach's rejection of molecules, and Einstein's later paper showing molecules exist.

segments.title: Skeptics, misuse of the razor, and ghosts
segments.summary: The hosts argue that a true skeptic uses the razor to consider alternatives, not to dismiss ideas. The ghost-in-photo example shows simplicity is subjective. Scientists use it in neural network decision trees as a practical choice, not proof of correctness.

segments.title: Creationism, atheism, nature, and art
segments.summary: Creationists and atheists both use the razor to argue for or against God. The hosts note nature is not necessarily simple, so simplicity is a human value. Geocentrism vs. heliocentrism shows the razor doesn't settle everything. Complexity in art is also subjective.

segments.title: Closing thoughts on Occam's Razor
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up that the razor is not meant to squash free thought and that complexity is not automatically wrong.

segments.title: Listener mail: North Korea Olympic medal tally
segments.summary: Claire Sutherland, editor of an Australian newspaper, describes how North Korea issued an official condemnation of her paper after it labeled North and South Korea as naughty and nice in its London Olympics medal tally graphic.
